user.title: Connect to EMHASS
user.description:
EMHASS Companion needs an existing EMHASS installation. Version {min_version} or newer is required.

If you run the EMHASS add-on, the address below is filled in for you.

data_description.url: For example http://192.168.1.10:5000. Filled in for you if you run the EMHASS add-on -- localhost only ever reaches Home Assistant itself.

reconfigure.title: Change the EMHASS address
reconfigure.description:
Version {min_version} or newer is required.

Everything else stays as configured -- reconfigure price, solar, load, tariff, battery or grid settings from the integration's own configuration options instead.

data_description.url: For example http://192.168.1.10:5000. Filled in for you if you run the EMHASS add-on -- localhost only ever reaches Home Assistant itself.

tariff.title: Buy and sell prices
tariff.description:
Your price source provides raw spot prices. Add whatever your supplier and grid operator charge on top, and what you are paid for exports.

Use **Linear** for VAT plus a fixed markup per kWh, **Already includes costs** if your price source already adds them, or **Template** for tiered or time-of-day pricing, which is entered under **Advanced settings**.

data_description.buy_multiplier: Multiplied with the spot price. Use 1.25 for 25% VAT.
data_description.buy_adder: Added after the multiplier. Grid fees, energy tax, supplier markup.
data_description.sell_adder: Added after the multiplier. Any per-kWh export compensation.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Price templates, only used when the method above is Template (the variables spot and time, your local time, are available), and the optional price forecast.

data_description.buy_template: Only used in Template mode. `spot` and `time` (your local time) are available.
data_description.sell_template: Only used in Template mode. `spot` and `time` (your local time) are available.
data_description.forecast_area: Your bidding zone as the source names it, for example SE2 or DE.
data_description.forecast_provider: Fills price hours your source has not published yet (for example tomorrow before the day-ahead auction) with a forecast, fitted to match your own prices. Off repeats the previous day instead. The key and area below are for the source chosen here. eupowerprices.com is for personal, non-commercial use only.

A sensor that already leaves out your deferrable loads; EMHASS learns from its history.

load_create.title: Create a house load sensor
load_create.description: Pick the sensor that measures your total house power. It should exclude the battery's own charge/discharge power -- EMHASS plans the battery separately, and counting its power here would throw off the load forecast. EMHASS Companion will create a new sensor that keeps this reading minus whatever your deferrable loads are drawing at any moment, and use that for the load forecast.

battery.description:
Leave this off if you have no home battery. Everything else on this page is then ignored.

{round_trip}

data.battery_power_invert: That sensor is positive when charging

data_description.no_discharge_to_grid: On blocks the battery from exporting and using arbitrage - house power is unaffected.
data_description.soc_min: The optimiser will not plan the battery below this level.
data_description.soc_entity: Read at the start of every run so the plan starts from reality.
data_description.battery_power_entity: What the battery is doing right now, for the dashboard cards to draw against the plan. Nothing in the optimisation reads it.
data_description.battery_power_invert: Leave off if the sensor is positive while discharging, which is the plan's own convention. Getting it the wrong way round labels a charging battery as discharging.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Charge taper, efficiencies, cycle and SOC costs, end-of-horizon SOC, self-consumption threshold and dynamic limits. The defaults suit most batteries.

data.charge_power_derating: Charge slower as the battery fills

data_description.charge_power_derating: Optional. A BMS often lowers the allowed charge current as the battery fills, so a plan that assumes full power the whole way starts too late and undershoots. Each row is "from this charge level, charge at most this percent of Maximum charge power". Leave empty to keep the flat maximum. Needs EMHASS 0.18.3 or newer; on an older add-on the table is kept but not sent.
data_description.weight_battery_discharge: What a kWh out of the battery costs you in wear, in the same currency as your prices. The optimiser adds it to every discharge, so it only empties the battery when the price spread it is chasing beats the cost. 0 means cycle freely; a rough starting point is the battery's price divided by its warranted lifetime throughput, often 0.02-0.10 per kWh.
data_description.weight_battery_charge: The same cost applied to a kWh into the battery. Leave at 0 if you already priced the whole round trip into the discharge cost above -- setting both charges each stored kWh twice.
data_description.battery_soc_deficit_threshold: The level below which the battery is charged a holding cost, if one is set below. Unlike Minimum charge level this is a preference, not a limit -- the plan may still go under when that is clearly worth it.
data_description.battery_soc_deficit_cost: Charged per kWh below the comfort level, per hour spent there, in your price currency. Nudges the plan to keep a reserve rather than sitting near empty. 0 turns this off, which is the default.
data_description.battery_soc_surplus_threshold: The level above which the battery is charged a holding cost, if one is set below. Sitting at full charge ages a lithium battery faster, so this discourages parking there for hours.
data_description.battery_soc_surplus_cost: Charged per kWh above the comfort level, per hour spent there. Use it to make the plan fill the battery late rather than early when both cost the same. 0 turns this off, which is the default.
data_description.battery_soc_final_reward_factor: How much a kWh left in the battery at the end of the plan is worth, as a share of the import price at that moment. 0 keeps the default: the plan aims for the End SOC target and sells anything above it. Raise it to let the plan keep spare energy instead; the End SOC target then becomes a minimum. Needs EMHASS 0.18.5 or newer.
data_description.battery_stress_segments: How finely the squared cost curve below is approximated. Higher tracks the true cost more closely but makes every optimisation a little slower; 10 is a good balance and only matters when a stress cost is set below.
data_description.battery_stress_cost: Discourages fast charging and discharging. The cost grows with the square of the power, so running at half power costs a quarter as much, and the plan spreads a charge over several hours instead of forcing it into the single cheapest one. Priced per kW at full power, per hour. 0 turns this off, which is the default.
data_description.end_soc_mode: How the battery level the plan aims for at the end of the horizon is chosen. "Optimized" computes it each run from the solar, price and load forecasts beyond the horizon; "Same as start" always plans back to the current level; "Fixed % slider" always aims for the Target charge level above. Requires EMHASS 0.18 or newer.
data_description.self_consume_threshold_w: When the plan's grid power is within this many watts of zero, the battery is handed to the inverter's own self-consumption mode instead of the plan's forced charge/discharge -- even a large planned charge or discharge is overridden, because self-consumption tracks real-time PV and load better than a forecast can at small imbalances. Once handed over, grid power must exceed twice this value before the plan can force the battery again, so it doesn't flip modes every recalculation. Not the same as the charge-level limits above, which only bound what the optimiser may plan between.
data_description.battery_first_priority: On prefers draining the battery before importing from the grid, so it is used up before any import while still above its minimum charge level. Mainly useful on a flat (non time-of-use) tariff. A soft preference, not a hard limit -- importing while the battery is charged is heavily penalised so drain-first wins on a flat tariff, but the optimiser can still import when that is the only feasible option, so it never makes a plan infeasible.
data_description.battery_dynamic: On caps how much the (dis)charge power may change between timesteps, using the two ramp limits below. Off leaves the battery free to swing between full charge and discharge power in a single step.
data_description.battery_dynamic_max: The most the discharge power may increase in one timestep, as a percentage of the battery's maximum power. Only takes effect once the ramp limit above is on.
data_description.battery_dynamic_min: The most the charge power may increase in one timestep, as a percentage of the battery's maximum power. Only takes effect once the ramp limit above is on.
data_description.soc_target: Where the optimiser aims to leave the battery at the end of the horizon. With End SOC set to "Optimized" this is instead the reserve floor the computed target never plans below; with "Fixed % slider" this is the exact level it aims for.
data_description.no_charge_from_grid: On restricts the battery to charging from excess PV only -- it will never buy grid power to charge. House power and export are unaffected.

inverter_settings.title: Inverter
inverter_settings.description: The inverter's own limits and losses. These apply whether or not you have a battery; without one only the maximum AC output matters.

data_description.hybrid_inverter: On if PV and the battery share one inverter's AC-side power limit, which is most home battery systems. Off if they are two independent inverters, each with its own limit.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Conversion efficiencies between DC and AC, and an optional live PV power sensor. The defaults suit most inverters.

data_description.pv_entity: Optional. Blended into the first step of every MPC forecast, weighted by the "Live value weight" number entity. Load is blended the same way automatically, using the sensor picked under House consumption > House load sensor -- no separate entity needed there.

inverter.title: Inverter profile
inverter.description:
How the battery is actually controlled. Leave this unset and the integration only ever reads.

Don't see your inverter? **Scripts** works with any inverter you can already control from Home Assistant, and advanced users can write their own YAML profile for a dedicated entry - see the profiles guide in the documentation.

Please report if you get an untested profile running on [Discord]({discord}).

Nothing is written to your hardware until you also turn on the Control enabled switch.

grid.title: Grid connection and schedule
grid.description: Your connection limits, and how often the plan is recalculated.{detected_resolution}

data_description.optimization_time_step: The step size EMHASS plans at. Matching your price source's own resolution (for example 15 minutes for current Nord Pool prices) captures the most detail; a coarser step solves faster. Pick from the list or type any number of minutes.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Curtailment, limit sensors and schedule timing. The defaults suit most houses.

data_description.grid_import_limit_entity: Leave empty unless your usable import limit moves. A sensor giving the limit in watts right now is used in place of the fixed number above — for a three-phase connection that is how you account for uneven phase loading, since the fuse that stops you is the worst phase's and the usable total is below the sum whenever the phases are unbalanced. Other uses: a load-balancing or dynamic-capacity system, a grid operator curtailment order. The sensor can only lower the fixed limit, never raise it, and the fixed number is used whenever it cannot be read. It is also raised back to the power the house is forecast to draw anyway if it ever falls below that, because no plan exists below that value.
data_description.grid_export_limit_entity: The same thing for export: a sensor giving the watts you may feed out right now, used in place of the fixed number above and only ever able to lower it. If EMHASS curtailment is off, be careful with a limit below your peak surplus solar — the optimiser then has nowhere to put that power and reports the problem as infeasible.
data_description.phase_l1_entity: Your meter's live reading for each phase, in W, kW or A. Current is best, since that is what the fuse reacts to. Together with the main fuse below, this replaces a hand-written import limit template. The plan gets the worst phase's limit automatically. With a battery power sensor set on the battery step, a forced charge is also cut within seconds if any phase gets close to its fuse. Fill in all three phases, or only L1 for a single-phase connection.
data_description.phase_l2_entity: The second phase. Any supported unit works, whatever L1 uses.
data_description.main_fuse_a: The rating of each main fuse, for example 16, 20 or 25 A. Leave empty to turn the phase guard off.
data_description.phase_margin_a: How far below the fuse rating every phase is kept. The default of 1 A covers meter delay, power factor, and a load switching on between two readings. A gG fuse (Diazed, Neozed) holds 1.25 times its rating for up to an hour, so a short overshoot while the guard reacts does no harm.
data_description.phase_voltage_v: Used to convert watt readings to current, and whenever the voltage sensor below is missing or can't be read. 230 V in most of Europe.
data_description.phase_voltage_entity: A live phase voltage from your meter, used instead of the fixed voltage above to convert watt readings to current. A heavily loaded phase sags, so the same watts are more amps. That is exactly when it matters. Use L1's voltage, or the lowest of the three if your meter has one. A reading more than 20% away from the fixed voltage is ignored and the fixed voltage is used instead, so a 400 V line-to-line sensor can't make the phases look emptier than they are. Not needed if your phase readings are in A.
data_description.phase_limit_window_min: The plan uses the lowest phase limit seen over this period, not the reading at the moment it is calculated. A dishwasher between heating cycles would otherwise hand the plan the whole fuse. 0 uses the live reading.
data_description.compute_curtailment: Turns on EMHASS's own curtailment (its compute_curtailment setting), sent with every run so it overrides whatever the add-on has stored. The optimiser is then free to shed solar it cannot use — the plan gains a curtailment column, and an inverter profile that supports curtailment follows it. Off by default, and only worth turning on if something can actually act on it: with no curtailment-capable inverter profile the plan assumes solar was shed that in reality still flows to the grid.
data_description.dayahead_fallback_time: A full day-ahead plan is normally rebuilt automatically as soon as new prices arrive. This time is only used as a backstop if that never happens.

compatibility.title: EMHASS entity names
compatibility.description:
Home Assistant already has EMHASS sensors:

{existing}

If your dashboards, templates or automations are written against those names, EMHASS Companion can publish its own plan sensors under the same entity ids, so they keep working.

Leave this off unless you need it -- the Companion's own names are clearer, and you can turn it on later under Configure.

data_description.emhass_standard_names: Renames the plan sensors to p_pv_forecast, p_load_forecast, p_grid_forecast, p_batt_forecast, soc_batt_forecast, optim_status, total_cost_fun_value, unit_load_cost and unit_prod_price, plus p_pv_curtailment and p_hybrid_inverter where you have those, and also publishes their forecast series in EMHASS's format. Per-load sensors are not renamed. Reversible.

error.cannot_connect: Could not reach EMHASS at that address. Check that it is running and that the address and port are correct.
error.unknown_version: Connected, but EMHASS did not report its version. It is probably too old.
error.version_too_old: This EMHASS is too old. Version {min_version} or newer is required, because this integration reads the plan through the JSON API introduced in that release.
error.ac_output_required: A shared inverter needs a positive AC output limit. Zero would block PV and the battery from reaching the house.
error.derating_not_ascending: Charge-taper rows must list strictly increasing charge levels, each between 1 and 99%, with a charge rate of 1–100% of maximum.
error.profile_required: Pick a solar forecast source, or open Advanced settings for the other choices.
error.template_required: Template mode needs a template. Enter it under Advanced settings, or pick another method.
error.phase_entities_incomplete: The phase guard needs all three phases, or only L1 for a single-phase connection.
error.phase_margin_too_large: The fuse margin must be smaller than the fuse rating.

abort.no_profiles: No usable data sources were found. This is unexpected; please report it.

data_description.forecast_provider: Fills price hours your source has not published yet (for example tomorrow before the day-ahead auction) with a forecast, fitted to match your own prices. Off repeats the previous day instead. The key and area below are for the source chosen here. eupowerprices.com is for personal, non-commercial use only.

inverter.title: Inverter profile
inverter.description:
How the battery is actually controlled. Leave this unset and the integration only ever reads.

Don't see your inverter? **Scripts** works with any inverter you can already control from Home Assistant, and advanced users can write their own YAML profile for a dedicated entry - see the profiles guide in the documentation.

Please report if you get an untested profile running on [Discord]({discord}).

Nothing is written to your hardware until you also turn on the Control enabled switch.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Parsing details and fixed option names. The defaults suit most setups.

data.energy_pattern_battery_first: Energy pattern: battery first option name
data.energy_pattern_load_first: Energy pattern: load first option name
data.work_mode_export: Work mode: export first option name
data.work_mode_zero_export: Work mode: zero export option name

data.grid_charge_disabled: Allow grid charge: disabled option name
data.direction_off: Battery control override: off option name

data.grid_charge_allowed_mode: Energy storage mode: grid charging allowed option name
data.mode_force_charge: Battery mode: force charge option name
data.mode_force_discharge: Battery mode: force discharge option name

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Other outdoor temperature sources.

data_description.profile:
1. EMHASS fetches it itself, with no weather integration. Needs your home location set in Home Assistant, and the solar forecast set to EMHASS built-in.
2. Reads a Celsius forecast from a list-valued attribute on any entity.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Parsing details and fixed option names. The defaults suit most setups.

network.title: Network tariff
network.description: Pick your grid operator's network tariff, or leave blank if you have a flat per-kWh fee. See the [documentation]({docs}) for what each profile does and how to add your own. Find and share ready-made profiles on [Discord]({discord}).

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Parsing details and fixed option names. The defaults suit most setups.

compatibility.title: EMHASS entity names
compatibility.description: Publish the plan sensors under the entity ids EMHASS itself uses, so dashboards, templates and other integrations written for EMHASS keep working. Off by default; turning it back off restores the names the sensors had before.{conflicts}

data_description.emhass_standard_names: Renames the plan sensors to p_pv_forecast, p_load_forecast, p_grid_forecast, p_batt_forecast, soc_batt_forecast, optim_status, total_cost_fun_value, unit_load_cost and unit_prod_price, plus p_pv_curtailment and p_hybrid_inverter where you have those, and also publishes their forecast series in EMHASS's format. Per-load sensors keep their own names -- EMHASS numbers those P_deferrable0, P_deferrable1 and so on by load order, and an entity id never moves once assigned, so adding or renaming a load would leave the number pointing at the wrong appliance.

metering.title: Cost and savings
metering.description:
Track what the grid actually cost you, and what solar and the battery saved against a house with neither. Measured from your own meters and your own prices — nothing here changes the optimisation.{found}

The meters were read from your Energy dashboard. They are stored when you submit, so reorganising that dashboard later cannot silently repoint them. Open *Meters* only if something above is wrong or missing.

data_description.metering_enabled: Creates the cost and savings sensors. Turning it off removes them and stops the tracking; the next 24 h forecast sensors are unaffected either way.

meters.name: Meters
meters.description: Override anything the Energy dashboard could not answer. Grid import and export are the only requirement — with them you get today's cost and today's saving, and adding solar splits that saving into a solar part and a battery part.

data_description.grid_import_energy_entity: Total energy bought from the grid. A daily counter that resets at midnight is fine.
data_description.grid_export_energy_entity: Total energy sold to the grid.
data_description.pv_energy_entity: Separates the solar saving from the battery saving. Your total saving does not depend on it — only the split between the two does.

advanced.title: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Limits for the optimiser's solver, sent with every run and overriding what is stored in EMHASS. The defaults suit most setups; raise the time limit if runs sometimes end without a feasible plan.

data_description.lp_solver_timeout: Seconds the solver may search before it must stop (lp_solver_timeout). Default 45, maximum 240 (the request to EMHASS gives up after 300). Long horizons or many deferrable loads and thermal tanks can need more.
data_description.lp_solver_mip_rel_gap: Relative gap at which the solver accepts a plan as good enough (lp_solver_mip_rel_gap). Default 0.01 = within 1% of the best possible cost. Lower finds a better plan but can take longer; higher finishes sooner.

error.ac_output_required: A shared inverter needs a positive AC output limit. Zero would block PV and the battery from reaching the house.
error.derating_not_ascending: Charge-taper rows must list strictly increasing charge levels, each between 1 and 99%, with a charge rate of 1–100% of maximum.
error.profile_required: Pick a solar forecast source, or open Advanced settings for the other choices.
error.template_required: Template mode needs a template. Enter it under Advanced settings, or pick another method.
error.phase_entities_incomplete: The phase guard needs all three phases, or only L1 for a single-phase connection.
error.phase_margin_too_large: The fuse margin must be smaller than the fuse rating.

single_constant.name: 11. Must run in one unbroken block

emhass_version_unsupported.title: EMHASS is too old
emhass_version_unsupported.description: EMHASS Companion needs version {required} or newer, but version {installed} is installed. It reads the optimisation plan through the JSON API added in {required}. Update the EMHASS add-on or container, then reload this integration.

invalid_profile.title: {count} data source profile(s) could not be loaded

plan_schema_unsupported.title: EMHASS plan format not understood
plan_schema_unsupported.description: EMHASS returned an optimisation plan using schema version {found}, but this integration understands major version {supported}. A new major version means columns were renamed or removed, or a unit or sign convention changed, so the plan is being ignored rather than misread. Update EMHASS Companion, or report this if no update is available.

thermal_comfort_unreachable.title: {name} cannot reach its comfort schedule
thermal_comfort_unreachable.description: At {heating_rate} °C/h, {name} cannot get from {current} °C to the {required} °C its schedule asks for by {time} -- the best it can do running flat out is {achievable} °C. This is checked with heat loss ignored, so the real shortfall is at least this big. Lower the comfort temperature, push the comfort window later, or raise the heating rate if it is set too conservatively for this load.

water_tank_behind_schedule.title: {name} cannot reach its hot-water target in time
water_tank_behind_schedule.description:
{name} is at {current} °C. With its {power} heater running flat out it reaches at most {achievable} °C by {time}, short of the {required} °C its schedule asks for then.

The plan is calculated with a lower target, so EMHASS still heats the tank as fast as it can. Asking for a temperature it cannot reach would make EMHASS find no plan at all. The tank catches up with its schedule on its own.

**What to do:** nothing, unless this keeps coming back. Then lower the required or lowest standby temperature, give the load more power, or check that the temperature sensor really belongs to this heater.

This clears automatically once the tank is on schedule.

optimization_infeasible.title: EMHASS could not find a feasible plan
optimization_infeasible.description:
The last {action} run reported the optimisation problem as infeasible, even after EMHASS retried with relaxed constraints. The previous plan is being kept instead of an unusable one. EMHASS Companion's own checks found no specific cause.

**What to do:** Download diagnostics from the integration's device page and run `scripts/check_infeasibility.py` on the file, and check the EMHASS add-on log.

This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_timestep0_defici.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: not enough power right now
optimization_infeasible_timestep0_defici.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: right now the plan needs at least {needed} ({pins} already running and held at that power, plus house {house}), but at most {available} is available (grid {grid}, solar {pv}, battery {battery}).

EMHASS cannot move a running load out of the first timestep, so it finds no plan at all. Usually the grid import limit has just dropped (a live fuse-limit sensor) while the battery is empty.

**What to do:** Turn off or lower one of the running loads, or check the grid import limit.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_battery_energy.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: battery too empty right now
optimization_infeasible_battery_energy.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: the battery is at {soc} (minimum {soc_min}), so over the next timestep it can deliver at most {battery}, not its rated {rated}. With the grid limited to {grid} and solar at {pv}, the house load of {house} cannot be covered.

**What to do:** Check the grid import limit, and that the battery level sensor reads correctly.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_pin_vs_window.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: a load is both running and parked
optimization_infeasible_pin_vs_window.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: {name} was reported as running at {power} right now, but the same request asked for no run time at all for it. EMHASS cannot satisfy both.

**What to do:** This is a bug in EMHASS Companion; please report it with a diagnostics download. Changing the load's mode or turning the load off usually clears it.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_window_too_short.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: {name} does not fit its window
optimization_infeasible_window_too_short.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: {name} needs {needed} timestep(s) to run {hours} h, but its window (timesteps {start} to {end}) only has {available}.

**What to do:** Shorten its run time, move its deadline later, or widen its allowed hours.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_window_energy.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: not enough energy before a deadline
optimization_infeasible_window_energy.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: within the next {hours} h the plan needs {needed} ({loads}, house {house}), but at most {available} can be supplied in that time (grid limit {grid} on average, solar {pv}, battery {battery}).

EMHASS must deliver each load's full run inside its window, so it finds no plan at all. Usually the grid import limit has dropped (a live fuse-limit sensor or the phase guard) during a long, high-power run.

**What to do:** Shorten the run, move its deadline later, or check the grid import limit.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_thermal_unreacha.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: {name} cannot reach its temperature in time
optimization_infeasible_thermal_unreacha.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: {name} must be at least {required} °C within {hours} h (timestep {timestep}), but it is at {current} °C and the best it can do with its heater at {power} the whole way is {achievable} °C.

EMHASS holds that temperature as a hard limit, so it finds no plan at all, and a tank that stays too cold is never heated because no plan is applied.

**What to do:** Lower the required or lowest standby temperature, give the load more power, or check that the temperature sensor really belongs to this heater.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_thermal_window.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: {name} cannot heat in time inside its window
optimization_infeasible_thermal_window.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: {name} must be at least {required} °C at timestep {timestep}, but its heating window only covers timesteps {start}-{end} and inside it the best it can reach is {achievable} °C.

EMHASS only lets a tank heat inside that window, and holds the temperature as a hard limit, so it finds no plan at all.

**What to do:** Widen the heating window, lower the required temperature, or turn the time window off for this tank.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_power_deficit.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: the house load cannot be supplied
optimization_infeasible_power_deficit.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: at {count} timestep(s) the forecast house load cannot be supplied even with grid import and battery discharge at their limits. Worst at timestep {timestep}: house {house}, solar {pv}, short by {short}.

**What to do:** Check the grid import limit, the battery and inverter power limits, and the house load forecast.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_pv_surplus.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: solar surplus has nowhere to go
optimization_infeasible_pv_surplus.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: at {count} timestep(s) the solar forecast exceeds what the battery, the house and grid export can absorb. Worst at timestep {timestep}: solar {pv}, house {house}, {excess} too much.

**What to do:** Enable PV curtailment in EMHASS, or check the grid export limit and the inverter limits.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_array_length.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: request arrays do not match
optimization_infeasible_array_length.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: the request's arrays disagree on length ({details}).

**What to do:** This is a bug in EMHASS Companion or in a data source profile; please report it with a diagnostics download.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

optimization_infeasible_forecast_nan.title: EMHASS plan infeasible: a forecast has gaps
optimization_infeasible_forecast_nan.description:
The last {action} run was infeasible: {key} has {count} empty value(s), the first at timestep {first}.

A data source returned nothing for part of the horizon; check the source behind that forecast.

The previous plan is being kept. {total} blocking cause(s) found in all; the Home Assistant log lists every finding. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

plan_degraded.title: EMHASS plan is a fallback, not a full solve
plan_degraded.description: The last {action} run did not finish a full solve, so EMHASS published a fallback plan (EMHASS status: {status}). The integration does not act on a fallback plan: while control is on, the battery goes back to self-consumption and deferrable loads are switched off until a full solve succeeds. Optimal (Incumbent) means the solver ran out of time and kept the best feasible plan it had: raise lp_solver_timeout in EMHASS, or shorten the optimisation horizon. Optimal (Relaxed) means the on/off decisions could not be solved, so EMHASS dropped them to find any plan at all. This resolves automatically once a full solve succeeds.

run_failed.title: The last {action} run failed
run_failed.description:
EMHASS did not produce a plan. The error it reported:

> {error}

**What to do:** if this does not clear after the next run, check the EMHASS add-on log for the full error.

The previous plan is being kept. This resolves automatically once a run succeeds again.

sources_blind.title: {count} source reading(s) have stopped reporting

pv_tail_short.title: Solar forecast ends too close to the horizon
pv_tail_short.description:
End SOC's Optimized mode has little or no solar forecast beyond the optimisation horizon, so it assumes darkness there and holds a conservatively high battery target.

Your Solcast profile can see one day further: open the integration's options, go to the solar forecast step, and add `{entity}` to the selected forecast sensors.

ml_forecaster_not_ready.title: Machine-learning load forecaster is not trained yet
ml_forecaster_not_ready.description:
The load profile is set to "Machine-learning forecaster", but it has not been confirmed trained for the currently configured sensor. Optimisation runs are using the sensor's own real recent readings meanwhile (its actual last day once there is one, its live reading repeated until then) so they keep succeeding and stay close to your household's actual consumption.

If the sensor has at least {days} days of history, a training run is triggered automatically -- no action needed. A brand new sensor (for example one just built by "Create a house load sensor") needs {days} days of real history to accumulate first. You can also press "Train load forecaster" yourself once it does. This resolves automatically once a fit succeeds.

script_control_entity.title: {count} load(s) use a script as their control entity

bad_stored_time.title: {count} stored time(s) could not be read

load_never_started.title: {name} never started
load_never_started.description:
{name} was requested and given its full {hours} h, but its power sensor never saw it draw anything. The request has been cleared, so nothing is waiting on it -- but the run did not happen.

Usual causes: the appliance needs its own start button pressed after being switched on, it does not resume its program when power returns, or the plug never actually powered it.

This clears itself the next time the load completes a run.

standard_names_taken.title: {count} EMHASS entity name(s) already taken

peak_tracking_off.title: Demand charge peak isn't tracked
peak_tracking_off.description: Your network tariff has a demand charge, but no grid import energy sensor is set, so the billing period peak can't be measured. The Billing period peak and Peak headroom sensors are not created, and the plan doesn't know how high this period's peak already is, so it can't tell which peaks would actually raise the bill. Turn on cost tracking and set a grid import energy sensor under Settings > Devices & services > EMHASS Companion > Configure > Cost and savings.

phase_clamp_off.title: Phase guard can't cut battery charging
phase_clamp_off.description: A main fuse is set on the grid step, but forced battery charging can't be limited in real time on this install. The plan's import limit from the phases still applies. See Dynamic grid limits in the documentation for what the clamp needs.

phase_clamp_off_no_battery_sensor.title: Phase guard can't cut battery charging
phase_clamp_off_no_battery_sensor.description: A main fuse is set on the grid step, but the battery has no power sensor. The guard has to measure what the battery is actually drawing. A charge the inverter hasn't started yet, or a discharge, would otherwise make the house look lighter than it is, and the guard would allow too much. Until a battery power sensor is set under Configure → Battery, forced charging isn't limited in real time. The plan's import limit from the phases still applies.

phase_clamp_off_slow_profile.title: Phase guard can't cut battery charging fast enough
phase_clamp_off_slow_profile.description: A main fuse is set on the grid step, but the inverter profile {profile} may only be written once every {interval} seconds. A cut held back that long can outlast what an overloaded fuse tolerates, so forced charging isn't limited in real time with this profile. The plan's import limit from the phases still applies. A profile that talks to the inverter locally, such as over Modbus, doesn't have this limit.

heat_topology_replaces_loads.title: EMHASS's heat topology replaces the Companion's loads
heat_topology_replaces_loads.description: The EMHASS add-on has a heat topology saved in its own configuration. EMHASS then replaces every load the Companion sends with the ones the topology builds, so the Companion's loads are not planned. Add "extend_deferrable_loads": true at the top level of the topology (needs EMHASS {required} or newer), or clear the topology in the add-on configuration. Then reload this integration.

heat_topology_replaces_loads_upgrade.title: EMHASS's heat topology replaces the Companion's loads
heat_topology_replaces_loads_upgrade.description: The EMHASS add-on has a heat topology saved in its own configuration. EMHASS then replaces every load the Companion sends with the ones the topology builds, so the Companion's loads are not planned. This EMHASS is older than {required}, the first version that can keep the Companion's loads next to a topology. Update the add-on and add "extend_deferrable_loads": true at the top level of the topology, or clear the topology in the add-on configuration. Then reload this integration.

water_tank_unsupported.title: Unsupported water tank backend
water_tank_unsupported.description: Water tank requires EMHASS {required} or newer. Detected version: {version}. Update EMHASS and ensure its version can be read. New optimisation and control are blocked; tanks are never treated as rooms.

water_tank_invalid.title: Invalid water tank data for {name}
water_tank_invalid.description: {name}: {reason}. New optimisation and control are blocked until tank settings and temperature sensor are valid. The device thermostat remains responsible for autonomous safe operation.

run_dayahead.name: Rebuild day-ahead plan
run_dayahead.description: Runs a full day-ahead optimisation over the whole planning horizon.

run_mpc.name: Recalculate now
run_mpc.description: Runs a model-predictive optimisation from the current state.

train_load_forecaster.name: Train load forecaster
train_load_forecaster.description: Trains EMHASS's machine-learning load forecaster on the load sensor's recent history. Only needed to retrain on demand: it trains itself once the sensor has enough history, and again every week. Fails if the load forecast method is not the machine-learning forecaster.

export_settings.name: Write settings to EMHASS
export_settings.description: Saves Companion's static settings (battery, inverter, solver, forecast and tariff defaults) into EMHASS's own configuration so its web UI and manual runs resemble Companion's. Unrelated EMHASS settings, such as connections and credentials, are kept, but values Companion manages itself are overwritten, including a saved heat topology and tariff settings. Live values such as state of charge, forecasts and temporary limits are never written. Administrators only.

test_profile.name: Test a data source profile
test_profile.description: Resolves a profile and returns what it produced, for diagnosing a source that returns nothing or the wrong values. Administrators only: the response includes the profile's resolved EMHASS settings.

options.name: Options
options.description: Options to resolve the profile with, validated against the profile's own options. Defaults to the configured ones.

limit.name: Limit
limit.description: How many series entries to include in the response.

typical_load_forecast.name: Typical household load forecast
typical_load_forecast.description: Backs the "Typical household" load profile. Returns one day's half-hourly load shape, scaled so its average matches the given power.

day.name: Day
day.description: The calendar day to forecast, in the local timezone.

average_w.name: Average power
average_w.description: The household's typical average power draw, in watts.

set_hot_water_plan.name: Set hot-water plan
set_hot_water_plan.description: Replace all daily periods and optimise without reloading.

periods.name: Periods
periods.description: 1–8 objects with draw_start, draw_end, draw_energy_kwh, and optional name and enabled.

user.title: Add a deferrable load
user.description: A load whose timing the optimiser may choose: a dishwasher, a car charger, a pool pump. What makes it want to run decides which settings it has, so it is asked first.

data_description.recurrence: Every day -- it needs a set number of hours every day, and the optimiser picks when. On demand -- it runs only when something arms it, for a set number of hours. On spare solar -- it takes whatever solar the house, the other loads and the battery are not already using, for as long as it is armed. A load on spare solar has no hours and no time window; both come from the plan. Spare solar is a Companion feature -- EMHASS has no such mode, so there is nothing to configure for it on the EMHASS side.

reconfigure.title: Edit deferrable load

data_description.power_sensor: Optional. The most reliable way to tell the optimiser whether this load is actually running -- catching a run that finished early, one that never happened despite being planned, or one started at a different time than scheduled. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit -- W, kW, MW, ... -- is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too, read the same way a control entity's state is. Without either and no control entity, the optimiser instead assumes the load followed its own last plan, which cannot see any of that.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations. With neither this nor a power sensor set, the optimiser instead trusts its own previous plan -- assuming the load ran whenever it was scheduled to. That is only as accurate as your own follow-through, so a real sensor or control entity is worth adding when you can.

reconfigure.description: Power, run time, the time window and the load model are controls on the load's own page, not settings here -- change them there or from an automation.

settings.title: Load settings
settings.description: These are the values the load starts with -- once it is added, each becomes a control on the load's own page that you can also change from an automation.

data_description.nominal_power_w: Roughly what this load draws while it is on.
data_description.operating_hours: How long it needs to run in total. The optimiser chooses when. EMHASS plans in {time_step}-minute steps, so this is rounded to the nearest whole step ({time_step_hours} h).
data_description.earliest_start: Only used if you turn on the load's time window switch afterwards.
data_description.latest_end: May be earlier than the start time, for an overnight window.
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether the load is actually running, so it can catch a run that finished early or never happened. A power sensor (any unit) gives the most detail; an on/off binary_sensor works too. Without one, the optimiser assumes the load followed its last plan.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan once you enable control, and its state also serves as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Minimum power, start and stop limits, and surplus tuning. The defaults suit most loads.

data.single_constant: Must run in one unbroken block

data_description.minimum_power_w: Only used when "Runs at full power only" is off.
data_description.semi_continuous: On for a dishwasher or pump, which are either on or off. Off for something whose power can be varied, such as a car charger.
data_description.startup_penalty: Discourages switching on and off repeatedly. Leave at zero unless that is a problem. On spare solar this is the right way to keep a load from short-cycling -- it prices a restart rather than forbidding a break, so the load still runs in one block on a clear day but may split across two peaks on a cloudy one.
data_description.single_constant: On if interrupting it would be a problem, such as a wash cycle.
data_description.minimum_on_time_minutes: Once switched on, the load must stay on at least this long. Protects compressor-driven loads (heat pumps, freezers) from short-cycling. Zero means no minimum.
data_description.minimum_off_time_minutes: Once switched off, the load must stay off at least this long. Zero means no minimum.
data_description.energy_needed_kwh: Optional total: the load stops asking once it has had this much. Leave at zero to let it run on whatever solar is spare until you turn its Requested switch off.
data_description.surplus_headroom_w: How much spare solar there must be beyond this load's own draw before a timestep counts. A margin against the solar forecast coming in light -- without it, a timestep counted at exactly this load's power imports as soon as a cloud arrives.
data_description.surplus_priority: Only matters with more than one load on spare solar. The lowest number claims the shared surplus first; ties are broken by name. Leave at zero unless you have several and want one served before another.
data_description.max_startups: A cap on how many times the load may switch on within one plan. Zero means no cap.

user.title: Add a thermal load
user.description: Choose a room for heating or cooling, or a water tank with one electric immersion element. The model is chosen at creation and cannot be changed later.

data_description.thermal_model: Room uses a measured heating rate. Room, advanced heat pump describes the building and lets EMHASS calculate heat pump efficiency and heat demand from the outdoor temperature. Both need an outdoor forecast; immersion water tank does not. Only a single immersion element is supported.

data_description.temperature_sensor: The room (or tank) the temperatures below apply to. Strongly recommended: without it, every plan starts from a guessed temperature instead of the actual one.
data_description.sense: Whether running this load raises the temperature (a heat pump, a heater, hot water) or lowers it (an air conditioner).
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether this load is actually running. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.
data_description.cop_curve: Optional. For a heat pump whose efficiency falls in the cold: pairs of outdoor temperature and COP, such as "7: 5.2, 0: 4.0, -10: 3.0". The heating rate is taken as measured at the first pair and is lowered to match the coldest hour of the forecast, so cold spells get more heating hours. Needs a weather entity as the temperature source. Leave empty to ignore. Heating only.

settings.title: Room settings
settings.description:
A load whose temperature the optimiser controls rather than its run time: a heat pump, direct electric heating, an air conditioner. Instead of "run N hours" you give a comfort band, and the optimiser finds the cheapest hours that keep the temperature inside it -- pre-heating into cheap electricity where the band allows.

These are the values the load starts with -- once it is added, each becomes a control on the load's own page that you can also change from an automation.

The model also needs an outdoor temperature forecast: set one under Configure > Outdoor temperature, or leave it to EMHASS if your solar forecast is EMHASS built-in (Open-Meteo).

data_description.temperature_sensor: The room temperature sensor. Without it, each plan starts from an estimated temperature.
data_description.sense: Whether running this load raises the temperature (a heat pump, a heater, hot water) or lowers it (an air conditioner).
data_description.nominal_power_w: Roughly what this load draws while it is on.
data_description.comfort_temperature: The temperature to hold while the comfort window is active. The optimiser may go above it when energy is cheap, never below.
data_description.setback_temperature: The lowest acceptable temperature outside the comfort window.
data_description.max_temperature: A hard ceiling that applies at all times. The gap between the comfort temperature and this ceiling is the storage the optimiser plays with -- heating a little extra while electricity is cheap.
data_description.comfort_start: When the comfort temperature starts applying each day.
data_description.comfort_end: When it stops and the setback takes over. May be earlier than the start time, for a window that crosses midnight.
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether this load is actually running. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: The room's heating and cooling behaviour. The defaults are a reasonable starting point.

data_description.heating_rate: How fast the temperature changes with the load running at full power. Watch a cold morning: a house that climbs from 18 to 21 °C in two hours with the heating flat out has a rate of 1.5 °C/h. For cooling, how fast it drops.
data_description.cooling_constant: How fast heat leaks to the outdoors: degrees lost per hour, per degree of difference to the outdoor temperature. Most homes land between 0.05 (well insulated) and 0.3 (draughty). If the planned heating comes too early, lower it; too late, raise it.
data_description.thermal_inertia: How long after switching on before the temperature responds. Underfloor heating in concrete can take an hour or more; a radiator or fan is nearly immediate. Leave at 0 if unsure.
data_description.cop_curve: Optional. For a heat pump whose efficiency falls in the cold: pairs of outdoor temperature and COP, such as "7: 5.2, 0: 4.0, -10: 3.0". The heating rate is taken as measured at the first pair and is lowered to match the coldest hour of the forecast, so cold spells get more heating hours. Needs a weather entity as the temperature source. Leave empty to ignore. Heating only.

water_tank.title: Immersion water tank
water_tank.description: One tank with one electric immersion element. Set the tank temperature limits and number of daily hot-water periods, then configure each period on the following pages. The optimiser chooses when to heat. No outdoor forecast is needed.

data_description.temperature_sensor: Required tank temperature sensor. Invalid or unavailable readings block new optimisation and control.
data_description.nominal_power_w: Roughly what this load draws while it is on.
data_description.comfort_temperature: Minimum tank temperature during each hot-water period. Water must be ready at the start. The optimiser may heat above this when electricity is cheap.
data_description.setback_temperature: Lowest acceptable tank temperature between hot-water periods.
data_description.max_temperature: Enter a safe ceiling for this tank and immersion element. Device thermostats and over-temperature protections remain authoritative.
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether this load is actually running. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.
data_description.hot_water_period_count: 1–8 daily periods. Enter times and estimated consumption on the following pages. Existing periods are retained when the count changes.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Standing heat loss, heater efficiency and how strictly the required temperature is kept. The defaults suit an immersion element.

data_description.standby_loss_w: Estimated constant standby heat loss in watts, not heater power. After setup, adjust on the load page or through automations.
data_description.heater_cop: Heat delivered per unit of electricity. 1 for an immersion element. For a heat-pump water heater use its seasonal COP at tank temperature, typically 2.5 to 3.5 and well below the headline rating. Power when running stays the electrical power.
data_description.comfort_penalty: 0 keeps the required hot-water temperature a hard limit. Above 0 it becomes a target: only the lowest standby temperature is a hard limit, and falling short of the target costs this much per degree and timestep. Higher is stricter: 1 or more acts like a hard limit, 0.1 to 0.5 lets the tank sag when electricity is expensive. Adds some solve time.

reconfigure_water_tank.title: Edit water tank

data_description.temperature_sensor: Required tank temperature sensor. Invalid or unavailable readings block new optimisation and control.
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether this load is actually running. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.
data_description.hot_water_period_count: 1–8 daily periods. Enter times and estimated consumption on the following pages. Existing periods are retained when the count changes.

reconfigure_water_tank.description: Edit tank volume and the number of daily hot-water periods, then review each period. Power, temperature limits and standby loss are adjusted on the load page. The model cannot be changed.

water_tank_period.title: Hot-water period {period} of {count}
water_tank_period.description: Hot water must be ready at the start and the required tank temperature maintained throughout. Estimated consumption is spread across this period each day, not shared across all periods. This is not a heater timer.

data_description.name: For example Morning or Evening.
data_description.draw_start: Daily start in local time. The water should already be hot at this time.
data_description.draw_end: May cross midnight. Equal start and end means a full day.
data_description.draw_energy_kwh: Estimated heat withdrawn during this period, in kWh, not heater electricity. Enter 0 for no expected withdrawal. Consumption from overlapping periods is added.

heat_pump_room.title: Room, advanced heat pump
heat_pump_room.description: A room or house heated by a heat pump. EMHASS calculates the heat pump's efficiency and the house's heat demand from the outdoor forecast, so no measured heating rate is needed. Heating only. Needs an outdoor temperature forecast the Companion can read, such as a weather entity.

data_description.temperature_sensor: Required. The plan starts from this reading.
data_description.nominal_power_w: Electrical power the heat pump draws while it runs. EMHASS multiplies it by the calculated COP.
data_description.comfort_temperature: Lowest room temperature during the comfort period.
data_description.setback_temperature: Lowest room temperature outside the comfort period.
data_description.max_temperature: Highest room temperature the optimiser may heat to.
data_description.comfort_start: Start of the daily comfort period.
data_description.comfort_end: End of the daily comfort period.
data_description.thermal_mass_m3: Volume of concrete-equivalent mass that stores the heat, in cubic metres. EMHASS uses concrete density and heat capacity. A larger value means the temperature changes more slowly.
data_description.floor_area_m2: Heated floor area in square metres.
data_description.specific_heating_demand: The building's yearly heat demand per square metre, in kWh/m², for a year with the annual heating degree days set under Advanced settings. Often 50 to 150 for a house.
data_description.supply_temperature: Water temperature the heat pump delivers to the radiators or floor heating. Lower means a higher COP. Typically 30 to 35 for floor heating and 45 to 55 for radiators.
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether this load is actually running. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.

advanced.name: Advanced settings
advanced.description: EMHASS model settings. The defaults suit most houses.

data_description.carnot_efficiency: How close the heat pump gets to the ideal Carnot COP. 0.4 is typical; EMHASS clips the resulting COP to 1-8.
data_description.constant_cop: Optional. A flat COP, for example the B0/W35 or B0/W45 figure from the heat pump manual. Overrides the Carnot calculation, so the outdoor temperature no longer affects the COP. It still drives the building's heat demand.
data_description.source_temperature: Optional. Cold-side temperature in °C for the COP, such as a typical brine temperature for a ground-source heat pump. Replaces the outdoor temperature in the Carnot formula, which still drives the heat demand. Ignored when a constant COP is set.
data_description.base_temperature: Outdoor temperature above which the house needs no heating.
data_description.annual_reference_hdd: Heating degree days of the year the specific heating demand refers to.
data_description.thermal_inertia_time_constant: Hours before delivered heat shows in the room temperature, such as for floor heating. 0 means immediately.
data_description.window_area: Optional. Effective glazing area in m², mainly south-, east- and west-facing windows. With a window area set, EMHASS adds window area × solar heat gain coefficient × solar irradiance to the heat the room gets, so a sunny day needs less heating. Needs EMHASS's solar irradiance forecast (it fetches this itself, with solar forecasting on). Leave empty for no solar gain.
data_description.shgc: Fraction of the sun's heat that gets through the glazing, 0 to 1. 0.6 suits modern double glazing. Only used with a window area.

error.invalid_tank_value: Enter a valid value; numbers must be finite and within the allowed range.
error.invalid_tank_band: Lowest standby temperature must not exceed required hot-water temperature, which must not exceed maximum temperature.
error.invalid_cop_curve: Enter at least two pairs of "outdoor temperature: COP", separated by commas, with a COP above 0 and each temperature listed once, such as "7: 5.2, 0: 4.0, -10: 3.0".
error.invalid_heat_pump_value: Enter a valid value; numbers must be finite and within the allowed range.
error.invalid_heat_pump_band: Setback temperature must not exceed comfort temperature, which must not exceed maximum temperature.

user.title: Add a load group
user.description: Group two or more existing deferrable loads that share a circuit -- a subpanel or fuse limit, or an EV charger and an immersion heater that must never run together.
